messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Samira is a 63-year-old auditor who lives alone in a quiet suburb, a widow by divorce rather than death, though the loss that shattered her was not of a spouse. As a girl in Detroit’s Middle Eastern community, she had been close to her younger brother Ali, who still lived nearby when he was killed twelve years ago. The event itself had unfolded in a way that made every subsequent survival instinct feel like a betrayal. Ali had been working a weekend shift at a city park maintenance facility when he was cornered by two men in a stolen van. By the time Samira arrived after frantic phone calls—she was the one he called first, the one who always knew what to do—he was already locked inside a small metal shed near the restrooms, bleeding from a stab wound. She had to force the padlock with a crowbar from her trunk. She remembered the smell of cut grass, the sound of her own screaming, the way the light fell through the dirty window onto his face. He died in her arms before the ambulance came. That moment had not ended. It continued, vividly, every time a door clicked shut behind her in a room without an exit, every time she drove past a patch of trees, every time she heard a news report about another victim of violence—Ali’s name never spoken, but his face imprinted on every stranger’s.

In the months afterward, Samira’s life began to reorganise itself around a single certainty: she could not trust the world to be safe, and she could not trust her own body to stop reacting as though the attack were still happening. Sleep, when it came at all, was a thin surface broken by violent starts—a replay of the shed, the crowbar, the weight of Ali’s head, the terror that was not memory but re-experience, complete with the same metallic taste in her mouth and the same crushing heat in her chest. She had no warning when it would happen. A glimpse of a locked storage closet at her office, the smell of damp soil in a landscaping bed by the parking lot, the sound of a key turning in a lock—any of these could drop her back into that afternoon with full sensory force. She learned to scan every new environment for exits and threats before she could focus on anything else. At work as an auditor, she had always been thorough, but now thoroughness became hypervigilance: she checked the lock on her cubicle door repeatedly, walked the perimeter of any new audit site before setting foot inside, and eventually refused assignments that required visiting unfamiliar offices. She told her supervisor she preferred to work from her own cubicle, where she could control the environment. Over the next years, she stopped accepting any fieldwork entirely, citing health reasons no one fully questioned. The consequence was quiet but real: she was passed over for a lead auditor position, and her colleagues began to see her as inflexible, even odd. Samira knew she was slowing down, but she could not explain that the unfamiliar was, for her, a place where danger lived invisibly, where she could not assess the risk until it was too late.

Her faith in people, in a benevolent order, had died in that shed. She stopped attending the mosque, stopped returning calls from Ali’s friends, stopped believing that any precaution mattered because, ultimately, she could not stop bad things from happening. She had tried. She had arrived and he still died. Her body, she felt, had betrayed her: even when she was safe in her own locked apartment, her heart pounded, her muscles tensed, her breath came shallowly, as if the threat were still immediate. She knew logically she was not in danger, but her body refused to believe it. What frightened her most was that the helplessness had spread: it was no longer just about that afternoon. It was about every locked door, every unfamiliar street, every reminder that she could not protect anyone, least of herself.

She came to therapy because last month, during a routine fire drill at work, the building’s safety protocol required everyone to remain enclosed in the stairwell for twenty minutes while maintenance checked the alarm panel. The moment the door clicked shut behind her, Samira was back in the shed, and she screamed until security officers escorted her out. Her supervisor gently suggested a leave of absence. Samira, ashamed and exhausted, finally agreed to see a clinician. She hopes, quietly, that she might be able to sleep without waking in terror, and that she might someday walk through a park without seeing her brother’s face. She is afraid that nothing will change—that her body and her mind have learned a lesson too deep to unlearn, and that the locked door of her own history will never open.
